---
title: "Gear 7: Violin Care for Beginners"
toc: true
toc-depth: 2
---

A violin is made of thin wood held under a lot of string tension. Looked after, it lasts centuries; a few minutes
a week of care keeps yours sounding and playing well. (The same goes for viola, and mostly for cello and bass.)

## Opening the case and holding it

- Lay the case **flat**, latches up, before opening. Close every latch and zip when you put it away; many violins
  are broken by falling out of a half-closed case.
- Pick the violin up by the **neck** or the edges, not the bridge or strings.
- Never leave it on a chair or the floor. In the case, or in your hands.

## The bow

- **Tighten** the hair before playing by turning the screw at the frog: until there's a gap about the width of a
  pencil between the hair and the stick at the middle. The stick should still curve **toward** the hair.
- **Loosen** it completely every time you put it away. A bow left tight warps.
- **Rosin**: a few strokes along the hair when the bow slides without gripping. New hair needs a lot; usually a few
  swipes per practice is plenty. Too much makes a scratchy sound and white dust.
- **Don't touch the hair**: skin oil stops the rosin working.
- Hair breaks now and then: snip it close to the ends, don't pull it out. When a lot is gone, it needs a **rehair**.

## Wiping down

After every practice, with a soft dry cloth:

- Wipe the **rosin dust** off the strings, the top under the strings, and the stick of the bow. Built-up rosin eats
  into the varnish.
- Wipe the strings and fingerboard.
- Never use furniture polish, alcohol or water on the varnish. Ask a luthier for proper cleaner.

## Tuning

- Use the **fine tuners** (small screws on the tailpiece) for small changes. Tighten = higher.
- **Pegs** are for larger changes: push in slightly while turning, so they hold. If pegs slip or stick, a teacher or
  luthier can treat them (peg compound).
- Tune A first, to A = 440 ([the strobe tuner](strobe-tuner.qmd)), then D, G and E.
- When fine tuners are screwed all the way in, back them out and bring the string up with the peg instead.

## The bridge

The bridge isn't glued; the strings hold it on. Tightening strings pulls its top toward the fingerboard.

- Check it every week or two from the side: it should stand **straight**, at a right angle to the top (the back
  face, toward the tailpiece, perpendicular).
- If it leans, a teacher can show you how to ease it back, holding it with both hands while the strings stay at pitch.
  If it falls, **loosen** all the strings and take it to your teacher: don't play without it.
- The **sound post** inside is wedged, not glued. If it falls (a rattle and a weak sound), loosen the strings and
  see a luthier.

## Strings

- Change a full set about every 6–12 months for regular players, sooner if they sound dull or won't stay in tune,
  or one is fraying.
- Change **one at a time**, so the bridge and sound post stay in place.
- New strings stretch for a day or two: retune often.

## Temperature and humidity

- Wood swells and shrinks with humidity. **Dry air** (winter heating) cracks violins and opens seams; very damp
  air makes pegs stick.
- Keep it at room temperature: never in a car, in the sun, or by a radiator.
- Aim for 40–60% humidity. In dry winters (north India), a case **humidifier** (such as a Dampit) helps.
- In the **monsoon** and humid coastal cities the danger is the other way: swollen wood, sticking pegs, rising
  action, softened glue and **mould** in the case. Use silica gel or a two-way humidity pack in the case, open the
  case to air in a dry room now and then, and don't keep it in a damp almirah or next to a wall.
- Air conditioners dry the air fast: don't leave the violin in the blast of an AC.
- Coming in from the cold: leave it in the closed case 15–30 minutes before opening.

## When to see a luthier

Open seams (a buzz, a gap at the edge), cracks, a warped bridge, a fallen sound post, slipping pegs, a bow that
won't tighten, or rehairs. Don't glue anything yourself.
